claims.text: HEA multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation because their chemically complex nanoscale interfaces act as dislocation barriers.
Dislocation blocking at multilayer interfaces inhibits creep and delays plastic flow.
The proposed coatings contain well-defined, chemically disordered interfaces between layers.
Thermal annealing can homogenize multilayer interfaces and diminish their structural and chemical complexity.
Sustained loading at moderate to elevated temperatures promotes creep in these coatings.
Nanoscale chemically complex interfaces induce residual stresses.
Nanoscale chemically complex interfaces impede dislocation climb.
Nanoscale chemically complex interfaces impede dislocation glide.
Complex chemical gradients at multilayer interfaces raise the local activation energy for dislocation-mediated deformation.
Residual stresses at multilayer interfaces raise the local activation energy for dislocation-mediated deformation.
Raising the local activation energy for dislocation-mediated deformation reduces the rate of time-dependent plastic flow.
Under identical creep testing, coatings with intact complex interfaces will have a significantly lower creep rate than interface-homogenized controls.
Coatings with intact complex interfaces will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to interface-homogenized controls.
The interface-barrier mechanism is expected to operate under moderate thermal and mechanical loads.
At extreme stresses or temperatures, the interface-barrier effect may be overcome.
At extreme stresses or temperatures, deformation mechanisms other than interface-limited dislocation motion may dominate.
